ann_17.original: Low-sodium hinge (two ReLU units in series) on serum sodium (mmol/L) and BMI (kg per square metre). The exit is zero at high sodium and across most of the normal range (2 of the 812 training rows with sodium of 139 mmol/L or more have it positive) and rises in a straight line as sodium falls below a BMI-dependent switch-on point, so the leaf reads as 'how far sodium is below the low end of the normal range, adjusted for BMI'. In the typical case (other inputs at their typical values) the exit is 0.00 at sodium 137, 0.46 at 136, 3.24 at 130 and 5.55 at 125. A higher BMI moves the switch-on point to a lower sodium: with BMI 20 the exit is still on at sodium 138 (0.10) and off at 139; with BMI 30 it is on at 136 (0.27) and off at 137; with BMI 40 it is on at 134 (0.43) and off at 135. On the training split the exit is positive for 495 of 1500 patients (outcome rate 30.7%, mean predicted risk 29%, against 45.1% and 46% for the rest), 406 of them among the 417 patients with sodium below 137 mmol/L. The leaf has no edge of its own to the output: it acts through the low-sodium arm (unit 1789), which is positive on 187 of these rows (the arm needs the hinge above about one unit before it switches on, so the hinge's weakest activations do not reach the prediction). Switching the leaf off (its exit replaced by its mean) lowers whole-model AUC from 0.857 to 0.821 and shifts the mean predicted risk by 0.036. Concept probe: '(137 - sodium) - 0.2 * (bmi - 27)' predicts the exit with score 1.00 (grade meaningful); '137 - sodium' alone scores 0.98; the U-shaped '(sodium - 137) ** 2' scores 0.29, confirming that this leaf is the low-sodium side only.
ann_17.proposed: A hinge on how far sodium is below about 133.8 mmol/L for a typical case, with a higher BMI moving the switch-on to a lower sodium.

ann_18.original: High-sodium steep hinge: one ReLU unit on serum sodium (mmol/L) with a small negative term from the noise column. The exit is zero across the low and normal range and rises in a straight line above the upper end of the normal range: in the typical case it is 0.00 at sodium 141, 0.027 at 142, 0.25 at 143, 0.69 at 145 and 1.80 at 150. The noise column shifts the switch-on point slightly: at sodium 142 the exit is 0.31 with noise -2, 0.027 with noise 0 and 0.00 with noise 2; at sodium 144 it is 0.76, 0.47 and 0.18 for the same three noise values. Its edge into the output weighs 3.22 (the first high-sodium hinge's weighs 1.61 and the low-sodium arm's 1.40), the heaviest edge into the output, so once it is on the risk climbs fast with sodium: whole-model risk in the typical case goes from 34% at sodium 142 to 92% at 145 and above 99% at 148 (part of that rise is the first high-sodium hinge in the sodium_U composition). On the training split the exit is positive for 334 patients (outcome rate 75.7%, mean predicted risk 76%, against 30.2% and 30% for the rest); none of them has sodium below 141 mmol/L (0 such rows), and 63 have sodium of 142 or less. Switching the leaf off lowers whole-model AUC from 0.857 to 0.839 and shifts the mean predicted risk by 0.047. Concept probe: 'sodium - 142' predicts the exit with score 0.99 (grade meaningful); the step 'sodium > 142' scores 0.98.
ann_18.proposed: A hinge that adds risk once sodium passes about 141.9 mmol/L, rising steadily above it.

ann_19.original: Three ReLU units in series, driven mainly by the noise column: the first rises with noise and, less, with sodium (both standardised); the second subtracts a large term for diabetes; the third subtracts a constant, so the exit is positive when the noise-plus-sodium signal is high and, with rare exceptions counted below, the patient is not diabetic. Described, not explained: the dominant input is the random noise column, so the leaf has no clinical reading. On the training split the exit is positive for 365 patients: 362 non-diabetic and 3 of the 441 diabetic patients. In a constructed low-sodium, high-noise case (sodium 130, noise 2.5) the exit is 1.70 for a non-diabetic and 0.00 for a diabetic patient, and the low-sodium arm it feeds is 1.51 against 2.11. Its only route to the prediction is a small negative edge into the low-sodium arm, and the exit and the arm are both positive on just 7 training rows. Switching the chain off leaves whole-model AUC at 0.8565 against 0.8565 (mean absolute risk change 0.0001): the chain is fitted noise with no practical effect. Concept probe: the best library concept, 'sodium * noise', scores 0.79 (grade partial); 'noise' alone 0.78; the ad hoc '(sodium - 139 + 4 * noise) * (1 - diabetes)' scores 0.95 but is a restatement of the unit's own gate, not a domain concept.

ann_20.original: Three ReLU units with two exits, driven mainly by the noise column: the first rises with noise and, less, with sodium (both standardised); the second (exit 7171) subtracts a large creatinine term, so it is on when creatinine is low and off when it is high; the third (exit 8285) is the second minus a constant. Described, not explained: the dominant input is the random noise column, so the leaf has no clinical reading beyond 'suppressed by high creatinine'. On the training split exit 7171 is positive for 892 patients, 27 of the 427 with creatinine above 100 umol/L; exit 8285 is positive for 568 patients, 6 of them with creatinine above 100. In a constructed low-sodium, high-noise case (sodium 130, noise 2.5) creatinine 50 gives exits 6.19 and 4.63, creatinine 90 gives 1.97 and 0.45, and creatinine 110 gives 0.00 and 0.00. Both exits enter the low-sodium arm with small negative weights, so in that constructed case the arm is 0.09 and the whole-model risk 11% at creatinine 50, against 2.22 and 85% at creatinine 110 (the direct creatinine edge adds to that difference). On the training split an exit and the arm are both positive on 83 rows (exit 7171) and 41 rows (exit 8285). Switching the chain off changes whole-model AUC from 0.857 to 0.853 and the mean predicted risk by -0.007. Concept probe: the best library concept is 'creatinine' with score 0.91 (grade meaningful), because the exits are gated off by high creatinine; 'noise' alone scores 0.27.
ann_20.proposed: A small chain on the random noise column, sodium and creatinine that lowers the predicted risk for the cases it acts on; higher creatinine closes it; its noise dependence is fitted noise.

ann_21.original: Serial composition: the low-sodium hinge feeds a final ReLU unit (1789) that also adds a small increment for smokers and for diabetic patients and subtracts the exits of the two noise chains, then a constant. The arm is the low-sodium side of the model's U-shaped response to serum sodium: it is silent at normal and high sodium and rises steeply as sodium falls below its switch-on point (located in the typical case below). On the training split the arm is positive for 187 patients (outcome rate 50.3%, mean predicted risk 49%, against 38.9% and 39% for the rest); it is never positive while the hinge is zero (0 such rows), and 12 of its rows have sodium of 135 mmol/L or more. In the typical case the arm switches on between sodium 135 (exit 0.00) and 134 (0.026), reaching 2.41 at 130 and 5.38 at 125; the whole-model risk is 10% at sodium 137, 39% at 132, 77% at 130 and 98% at 127. At sodium 130 smoking raises the arm's exit from 2.41 to 2.69 and diabetes to 2.82 (both: 3.10); the whole-model risk for the four cases is 77%, 93%, 92% and 98%, most of that from the direct smoker and diabetes edges in the root. Through this arm alone the smoker edge weighs 0.122 and the diabetes edge 0.188 per standardised unit. The noise chains pull the arm down when the noise column is high: at sodium 130, noise 1 leaves the exit at 2.41 (risk 80%) while noise 3 lowers it to 1.06 (risk 46%); switching the three chain edges off changes AUC from 0.8565 to 0.8538. Switching the whole arm off lowers AUC from 0.857 to 0.821 and shifts the mean predicted risk by 0.036.
ann_21.proposed: An arm that adds risk as sodium falls below about 133.9 mmol/L; a higher BMI moves the switch-on lower, and smoking and diabetes add a little within it.

ann_22.original: Parallel composition of the model's U-shaped response to serum sodium, with three exits into the output: the low-sodium arm (unit 1789, output weight 1.40), a first high-sodium hinge (unit 219, weight 1.61) and the steep high-sodium hinge (unit 1180, weight 3.22). The first high-sodium hinge switches on just above the middle of the normal range and rises linearly with sodium, with a small extra for men: in the typical case it is 0.00 at sodium 137 for women and 0.00 for men, 0.017 and 0.14 at 138, 0.39 and 0.51 at 140, and 2.25 and 2.37 at 150; the male edge weighs 0.062 per standardised unit and switching it off changes AUC from 0.8565 to 0.8557. On the training split this hinge is positive for 945 patients, including 812 of the 812 with sodium of 139 mmol/L or more and 133 of the 688 with sodium of 138 or less; it is also positive on 334 of the 334 rows where the steep hinge is positive. The low and high arms never act on the same patient: 0 training rows have both the low-sodium arm and the first high-sodium hinge positive, and 0 have the arm and the steep hinge positive. The low-sodium arm also feeds the first high-sodium hinge through an edge of weight 0.0087, whose removal changes the predicted risk by 0.0002 on average (mean absolute change); with 0 training rows where both are positive, that edge is inert on the training data. Between sodium 135 and 137 mmol/L, 316 of the 328 training patients have all three exits at zero; across the whole split 368 patients have all three at zero, with outcome rate 19.0% and mean predicted risk 19%. The U in the typical case (whole model): risk above 99% at sodium 125, 77% at 130, 22% at 133, 10% at 135 and 10% at 137 (the floor), then 21% at 140, 59% at 143, 92% at 145 and above 99% at 150. The high side is steeper and starts closer to the floor than the low side. By sodium band on the training split: below 135 mmol/L 227 patients, outcome rate 44.1%, mean predicted risk 43%; 135 to 142, 998 patients, 28.2% and 28%; above 142, 275 patients, 81.5% and 82%. Switching the whole composition off lowers AUC from 0.857 to 0.697 and shifts the mean predicted risk by 0.204; the first high-sodium hinge alone is worth 0.857 to 0.831.
ann_22.proposed: Serum sodium acts in a U shape, with the predicted risk lowest at about 134.5 mmol/L and higher either side, steeper on the high side above about 141.9 mmol/L.

ann_23.original: Root: the predicted risk is the sigmoid of a sum of six direct terms, the three exits of the sodium_U composition and a negative bias. Each direct term is positive, so on its own edge each input raises the risk: per standardised unit, age weighs 0.79, BMI 0.38, creatinine 0.36, smoker 0.40, diabetes 0.28 and the noise column 0.17; switching all six off (each replaced by its mean contribution) lowers AUC from 0.857 to 0.767. Whole-model sweeps in the typical case: age 30 gives risk 2%, age 60 15% and age 90 57%; BMI 18 gives 9% and BMI 40 34% (BMI also shifts the low-sodium hinge, which is off in this case); creatinine 50 gives 11%, 120 24% and 300 77%; a non-smoking non-diabetic patient 16%, diabetes alone 27%, smoking alone 33%, both 48% (whole-model values; smoking and diabetes also enter the low-sodium arm, which is off here); the noise column -2 gives 12% and 2 21%. Systolic blood pressure and heart rate have no enabled connections and no effect: the risk is 16% at systolic pressure 90, 16% at 145 and 16% at 200 mmHg, and 16%, 16% and 16% at heart rates 50, 85 and 120. The sodium_U composition is the model's main nonlinear structure: switching it off lowers AUC from 0.857 to 0.697, more than the six direct terms together. On the training split the outcome rate is 40.3% over 1500 patients and the model's AUC 0.857 with accuracy 0.775.
ann_23.proposed: The model adds a U shape over sodium to six inputs that each count on their own (age, smoking, diabetes, creatinine, BMI and the random noise column); it ignores heart rate and systolic blood pressure.

The exit is zero at high sodium and across most of the normal range (2 of the 812 training rows with sodium of 139 mmol/L or more have it positive) and rises in a straight line as sodium falls below a BMI-dependent switch-on point, so the leaf reads as 'how far sodium is below the low end of the normal range, adjusted for BMI'. In the typical case (other inputs at their typical values) the exit is 0.00 at sodium 137, 0.46 at 136, 3.24 at 130 and 5.55 at 125. A higher BMI moves the switch-on point to a lower sodium: with BMI 20 the exit is still on at sodium 138 (0.10) and off at 139; with BMI 30 it is on at 136 (0.27) and off at 137; with BMI 40 it is on at 134 (0.43) and off at 135. On the training split the exit is positive for 495 of 1500 patients (outcome rate 30.7%, mean predicted risk 29%, against 45.1% and 46% for the rest), 406 of them among the 417 patients with sodium below 137 mmol/L. The leaf has no edge of its own to the output: it acts through the low-sodium arm (unit 1789), which is positive on 187 of these rows (the arm needs the hinge above about one unit before it switches on, so the hinge's weakest activations do not reach the prediction).
